Explanation

Your application has hardcoded URLs that might correspond to services that are not accessible on Azure.

Review and ensure that the application is attempting to access URLs that would be available from Azure. You might need to migrate those services to Azure too, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.

If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premises, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.
Local or network IO operations detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.csLine 57
src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.csLine 57

Explanation

Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.
Local OS environment access detected
 Potential 1
FilePosition
src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.csLine 56
src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.csLine 56

Explanation

Local OS environment access detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, Read config via App Settings or App Configuration; avoid machine‑specific environment APIs. Persist environment setup via install scripts when needed.

When running in Azure App Service environment, your application can read environment variables that you define in App Service settings. Using environment API other than reading environment variables might indicate that your application depends on some local machine's features and might be broken on App Service sandbox or not scale well. Review your scenarios and either refactor them to be more cloud friendly or choose the option in App Service to host your application in the sandbox for Windows Container Web Apps.

If you choose to use other Azure hosting options such as Azure Container Apps (ACA) or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), environment APIs might work, however scaling still might be an issue.
SQL database connection detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config

Explanation

SQL database connection detected.

Ensure the database is available/reachable on Azure.

If it is not, there are multiple ways you can move your data to Azure:
1. Migrate to Azure SQL Database.
2. Consider Azure SQL Managed Instance if you need features that are not available in Azure SQL Database and you don’t want to use a VM.
3. Migrate your database servers directly to SQL Server on Azure VMs.

To assess database migration effort, you can use Azure Migrate tool, see the link below.

Explanation

Connection strings without configuration builders detected.

Keeping connection strings directly in the app is not the best practice and might introduce security risks, increased maintenance, scalability challenges or compliance standards (such as PCI DSS, GDPR, etc.).

Instead, it is recommended to use configuration builders to get secrets from secure sources in Azure environment.

Your current approach of serving static content directly might lead to increased costs, performance issues, maintenance challenges (requiring application redeployment for content changes), and security risks.

Consider moving static content to Azure Blob Storage and adding Azure CDN.
Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience
 Optional 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\eShopWCFService.csproj

Explanation

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, validate on .NET Framework 4.8 or move to .NET 10. Persist any runtime prerequisites via install scripts; test in staging before production.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

Application targeting .NET framework lower than 4.7.1 might missing features that would be needed for some cloud scenarios like scaling or getting secrets from secure external sources.

Azure App Service runs apps on .NET Framework 4.8 or .NET Framework 3.5. Apps running on on .NET Framework versions older than .NET Framework 4.8 could have potential compatibility issues. It is recommended to test your application running on .NET Framework 4.8. Note that it is not necessary to re-target to .NET Framework 4.8, only to validate that the app correctly runs on that version of .NET Framework.

In the long term it is also recommended to upgrade your application to latest supported .NET 8+ which would significantly increase performance of your application. Use tools like .NET Upgrade Assistant to help with upgrading your application to newer .NET.
System.Data.SqlClient dependency detected
 Optional 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config

Explanation

System.Data.SqlClient dependency is detected.

While System.Data.SqlClient will work in Azure, the newer Microsoft.Data.SqlClient package is the primary .NET SQL client moving forward and receiving the latest features. For example, Microsoft.Data.SqlClient easily allows use of Azure Managed Identity from a connection string.

Explanation

API is binary incompatible for selected .NET version: affects existing binaries, often requiring recompilation, because the API has changed in a way that prevents older binaries from loading or executing.
Project's target framework(s) needs to be changed
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\eShopWCFService.csproj
src\eShopWinForms\eShopWinForms.csproj

Explanation

Project's target framework(s) needs to be changed to the new target framework that you selected for this upgrade.

During upgrade target framework will be adjusted to corresponding platform when applicable. In some cases project would result in multiple target frameworks after the upgrade if it was using features that now have their own platforms in modern .NET frameworks (windows, iOS, Android etc).
Project file needs to be converted to SDK-style
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\eShopWCFService.csproj

Explanation

Project file needs to be converted to SDK-style. Modern .NET framework projects require a change in the project file format and use SDK corresponding to project flavor and functionality.
WCF Client APIs
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition

Explanation

WCF client-side APIs for building service clients that communicate with WCF services. These APIs are available as exact equivalents via NuGet packages - add System.ServiceModel.* NuGet packages (System.ServiceModel.Http, System.ServiceModel.Primitives, System.ServiceModel.NetTcp, etc.)
Legacy Configuration System
 Mandatory 2
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy XML-based configuration system (app.config/web.config) that has been replaced by a more flexible configuration model in .NET Core. The old system was rigid and XML-based. Migrate to Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration with JSON/environment variables; use System.Configuration.ConfigurationManager NuGet package as interim bridge if needed.
GDI+ / System.Drawing
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition

Explanation

System.Drawing APIs for 2D graphics, imaging, and printing that are available via NuGet package System.Drawing.Common. Note: Not recommended for server scenarios due to Windows dependencies; consider cross-platform alternatives like SkiaSharp or ImageSharp for new code.
Windows Forms Legacy Controls
 Mandatory 3
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy Windows Forms controls that have been removed from .NET Core/5+ including StatusBar, DataGrid, ContextMenu, MainMenu, MenuItem, and ToolBar. These controls were replaced by more modern alternatives. Use ToolStrip, MenuStrip, ContextMenuStrip, and DataGridView instead.
Windows Forms
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition

Explanation

Architecture Diagram

Source-based assessment of eShopModernizedNTier only. “Active” means selected by the checked-in solution and startup wiring, not a verified running deployment.

Application Architecture

flowchart TD subgraph Client["Desktop presentation - NET 6 Windows"] User["Catalog operator"] Desktop["WinForms desktop application"] Assets["Local catalog image files"] end subgraph Server["Windows IIS - WCF service"] Soap["SOAP over HTTP"] Logic["Catalog and stock business operations"] EF["Entity Framework 6.1.3"] end subgraph Storage["Persistence alternatives"] ContainerDB[("SQL Server Windows developer container")] LocalDB[("SQL Server LocalDB fallback")] end User -->|"browse and manage availability"| Desktop Assets -->|"load images from local disk"| Desktop Desktop -->|"synchronous SOAP requests"| Soap Soap -->|"dispatch operations"| Logic Logic -->|"query and save"| EF EF -->|"environment connection override"| ContainerDB EF -.->|"when override absent"| LocalDB

The solution selects the SDK-style desktop project and the classic WCF project [A1]. The desktop constructs the generated service client directly; the .svc host selects the database-backed service [A2, A3]. Compose describes the SQL Server container alternative, while connection selection falls back to the configured LocalDB database [A4, A5].

Technology Stack Summary

LayerTechnologyVersionPurpose
Presentation, activeWinForms with Windows desktop SDK; WPF also enablednet6.0-windowsDesktop UI; WPF enablement is a build setting, not proof of WPF screens [A6]
Presentation, alternateClassic WinForms project.NET Framework 4.7.1eShopWinForms.fx.csproj, not selected by this solution [A1, A7]
ServiceWCF, IIS, classic ASP.NET hostingProject target .NET Framework 4.6.1SOAP service; not ASP.NET Core or REST [A8]
Container runtime imageWCF on .NET FrameworkImage tag 4.7.2Hosting image differs from service compilation target [A9]
PersistenceEntity Framework and SQL Server provider6.1.3 on server; 6.4.4 declared on clientServer DbContext; client package does not establish client database access [A6, A10]
StorageSQL Server Windows developer image / LocalDBSQL image untagged; engine version not pinnedPersistent service data [A4, A5]

Data Storage & External Services

One service owns the catalog database. There is no source-evidenced broker, distributed cache, gateway, or external business API in the traced execution path. Catalog images are read from the desktop filesystem, not fetched from the WCF host [A11]. Compose exposes the WCF and SQL containers, but the desktop is not containerized [A4].

Key Architectural Decisions

  • The desktop view raises events to a controller, which makes synchronous WCF calls; application startup uses manual construction, not active dependency injection [A2, A12].
  • The service accesses EF directly rather than through a repository layer; initialization creates and seeds a missing database [A3, A10].
  • CatalogServiceMock is an alternative in-memory implementation, not an automatic outage fallback. ApplicationModule registrations are commented out; its mock flag does not control active startup [A2, A13].

DTOs & Contracts

CatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogType, CatalogItemsStock and DiscountItem are mutable service-level DataContract classes; entities double as transport contracts. Generated client copies are separate types; server lists become client arrays. No gateway aggregation DTO, OpenAPI, protobuf or GraphQL contract is evidenced in this scoped service. WCF data-contract serialization is used, not JSON. See data-architecture.md for fields and persistence details [S1, S2, S8].

Communication Patterns

  • Synchronous: UI controller calls generated WCF proxy methods; service queries EF in-process. UI loads service data before displaying the dialog [S3, S9].
  • No async transport: generated Task wrappers exist, but no queue, event choreography, discovery registration, gateway, load balancing, or retry/circuit-breaker policy is evidenced by the traced code [S2, S7, S9].
  • Timeouts: no explicit timeout values are set in generated binding construction or service endpoint configuration; WCF defaults apply. Client receive/buffer limits are int.MaxValue, reader quotas are maximal, and cookies are enabled [S10].
  • Discovery/configuration: active default client address is compiled into the generated proxy as localhost HTTP. Editing legacy App.config alone does not change that generated constructor's selected address [S3, S10].
  • Failure handling: no controller catch/retry or automatic switch to mock. The mock's discount operation throws; it is not operationally equivalent to the database service [S9, S11].
  • Startup: database availability affects first service data access; Compose start ordering is not a guaranteed healthy dependency gate. Details belong to configuration-inventory.md [S5].
  • Security posture: active client and explicit service endpoint use basic HTTP without configured transport security or application authentication/authorization. No role/resource checks appear in the traced operations. A separate HTTPS protocol mapping is present but does not establish TLS on the active HTTP deployment. Hosting/network restrictions outside source remain unverified [S6, S7, S10].

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. An existing Windows-compatible external nat network is referenced, not created by root Compose [C7].
  2. eshopwcfservice declares depends_on: sql.data. SQL has a healthcheck at 1-second interval with 20 retries; there is no service_healthy condition or application retry loop, so start ordering is not proof SQL is ready. Timeout/start-period values are not explicitly set [C7].
  3. EF initialization is registered in the DbContext constructor and runs on database initialization/access, creating and seeding only a missing database [C6, C15].
  4. Desktop startup calls LoadView before showing its modal dialog, so service/data/image failures can prevent a usable initial view. No explicit wait/readiness loop is present [C14].

Core Business Workflows

The desktop application lets an operator browse products by brand/type, see date-dependent sale prices, query stock for a selected day, and record or replace dated availability. This scope contains no checkout, order placement, payment, or shipping execution workflow; “shipment” is the UI's name for a dated stock record [B1, B2].

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
CatalogItemCatalogService / catalog managementProduct offered for displayBelongs to brand and type; logical target for stock records
CatalogBrandCatalogService / catalog classificationProduct brand filter choiceClassifies products
CatalogTypeCatalogService / catalog classificationProduct category filter choiceClassifies products
CatalogItemsStockCatalogService / inventory availabilityAvailable quantity for one product on a dayLogical product link; not a shipment lifecycle aggregate
DiscountItemCatalogService / promotionsGlobal time-bounded price reductionApplied by desktop to displayed catalog prices; no product-specific association

Business meaning is inferred from entity declarations and consuming code [B1-B4]. Persistence field details and relationship enforcement belong to data-architecture.md.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
CatalogServiceCatalog, dated availability, promotionsAll five domain entitiesDatabase through EntityModel
eShopWinFormsOperator interaction, display compositionNo authoritative stored domain entitiesGenerated WCF service contract and local image files
CatalogServiceMock, inactive alternativeIn-memory demonstration dataCopies of catalog/classification/stock statePreconfigured data; discount unsupported

These are application tiers, not independently owned microservice bounded contexts. The .svc host selects the database implementation; startup selects a remote generated proxy, not the mock. The alternate .fx.csproj is not selected by this solution [B5-B7].

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Initial catalog load and filtered sale-price display

  1. Startup creates the view, WCF proxy and controller; LoadView runs before the dialog is shown [B5].
  2. Controller checks today's discount for the banner, loads catalog products and separately queries today's discount again for price display, loads brands/types, then loads the unfiltered product list for stock controls [B1:60-85,88-157].
  3. Brand/type dropdown changes raise filter events. Service applies the All-filter rule; view combines returned products with the discount fraction and local image files [B1:27-29,75-85; B2:48-61,106-135; B3:56-62].
  4. Promotion-window rule selects the first matching discount. With no current promotion, displayed prices use the original price. Seed promotions are historical 2017 data, not evidence of a sale at assessment time [B1:60-85; B3:28-30; B8:41-51].

No gateway performs this composition: the desktop joins a product response and global discount response. Responses are independent calls, not a transactionally consistent snapshot [B1:75-85].

Workflow 2: Record or replace availability

  1. Operator selects a product and enters quantity/date. View applies the Shipment-input guard before raising an availability event [B2:157-167].
  2. Controller constructs a stock contract and synchronously submits it; service searches for that product on the same calendar day [B1:35-43; B3:99-102].
  3. Stock-replacement rule: replace the existing row's quantity, otherwise allocate a new stock ID and add a row; save changes [B3:104-117].
  4. On successful return, view shows a confirmation and clears inputs. No automatic availability-search refresh is performed in this handler [B1:42-43; B2:189-195].

This replaces a snapshot quantity; it does not increment stock, reserve inventory, or initiate shipment delivery.

Workflow 3: Query availability for a selected day

  1. Operator selects a product from the list and a calendar day. View extracts the product ID and raises a search event [B2:142-151].
  2. Controller requests availability. Database service selects the first matching dated stock row and returns quantity or zero [B1:50-54; B3:90-96].
  3. View appends a result row to the list; it does not replace previous search history [B2:173-182].

Mock behavior differs: a missing stock row is dereferenced rather than safely returning zero, and discount lookup throws NotImplementedException. Mock is not a resilient substitute for these active workflows [B7].

Workflow 4: First-use business data initialization

When a database is absent, its initializer seeds classifications, products, dated stock, and promotions. This is setup state, not a scheduled replenishment or promotion-update job; existing databases are not reseeded by this initializer [B8, B9].

The SOAP contract also exposes product create/update/remove operations, but the inspected controller does not initiate them. Do not equate public service CRUD with implemented desktop editing screens [B1, B10].

Cross-Service Data Flows

The only traced inter-process business exchange is desktop ↔ CatalogService; the service accesses its own database. Desktop composes products and the global promotion, and resolves product image filenames against local files. Classification dropdowns are built from separate brand/type responses, adding an All choice locally. There are no broker events, gateway aggregation, compensating actions or downstream partial-result fallbacks in the inspected path [B1, B2, B3].

Service or database failure propagates through unguarded synchronous controller calls. The application does not automatically return stale catalog data or switch to mock mode; startup data loading happens before the modal UI appears [B1, B5, B6].

Business Workflow Sequence

Business Rules & Decision Logic

RuleObserved behavior and limitsEvidence
All-filter ruleID zero means no filter; nonzero brand/type conditions are combined with AND; products materialized before filteringB3:56-62
Promotion-window ruleStart and end are inclusive calendar days; first matching discount wins with no explicit ordering/overlap arbitrationB3:28-30
Sale-price calculationDisplay uses original price multiplied by one minus discount fraction, converted to double and formatted; banner rounds fraction times 100. No bounded fraction validation or stored price mutation shownB1:60-85; B2:48-61
Shipment-input guardMissing product, empty quantity or empty date returns silently; quantity parsed as int, date by Convert.ToDateTime. No TryParse, nonnegative quantity check or date-range rule shownB2:157-167
Search-input assumptionSelected stock-search item is dereferenced without null guard; ID parsed from display stringB2:142-150
Stock-replacement ruleFirst row matching item/calendar day is overwritten, not summed; missing row receives maximum StockId plus oneB3:99-117
Availability absenceDatabase implementation returns zero; mock can fail on absent rowB3:90-96; B7:95-98
Identifier ruleNew product and stock IDs use maximum plus one; no empty-set handling or concurrency-safe allocator on this pathB3:65-70,113-116
Classification text ruleBrand and type have maximum length 50; no dedicated domain validator appears in traced serviceB4

State transitions: stock is inserted or replaced; there is no shipment/order status machine. Product CRUD persists supplied state without a domain approval workflow [B3].

Transactions and integrity: separate SaveChanges calls establish persistence boundaries. There is no explicit cross-call transaction, saga or compensation for the desktop sequence, stock read/write allocation, or multi-stage seeding; no explicit unique item/date constraint is declared in the stock entity [B3, B9, B11].

Error handling, audit and authorization: no business exception hierarchy, local catch/retry, business audit log, or role/ownership check is present in the inspected controller/service flows. UI notification follows a successful call, not a verified distributed transaction. Image-loading/parse errors are likewise unhandled in the traced view methods [B1-B3]. Hosting and infrastructure access controls outside source are not assessed.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The selected client targets .NET 6 and the service targets .NET Framework 4.6.1, both older runtime targets requiring support/compatibility review. Server EF 6.1.3 differs from the client's 6.4.4 declaration; EF6 is not EF Core. The classic server depends on Visual Studio WebApplication MSBuild targets and package HintPaths, while the desktop is SDK-style [D1-D3]. These are source-observed compatibility concerns, not a vulnerability scan or a restored transitive dependency analysis.

Entity Model

erDiagram CatalogBrand ||--o{ CatalogItem : "classifies" CatalogType ||--o{ CatalogItem : "classifies" CatalogItem ||--o{ CatalogItemsStock : "logical item reference only" CatalogBrand { int Id PK string Brand "maximum length 50" } CatalogType { int Id PK string Type "maximum length 50" } CatalogItem { int Id PK string Description string Name decimal Price "money with precision 19 and scale 4" string Picturefilename int CatalogBrandId FK int CatalogTypeId FK } CatalogItemsStock { int StockId PK date Date int CatalogItemId "logical reference not explicit ORM FK" int AvailableStock } DiscountItem { int Id PK double Size date Start date End }

All entities are owned by the catalog service [P1]. Product-to-brand/type navigation is unidirectional from product; no inverse collection is declared. Non-null integer references imply required relationships by EF conventions, but explicit cascade configuration and deployed constraints are not shown. The stock relationship is logical only: a scalar item ID without a navigation property, ForeignKey annotation or fluent relationship does not establish an EF/database FK. DiscountItem has no mapped relationship to products [P7-P10].

Brand/type IDs and product IDs are non-database-generated. Stock uses explicit non-generated StockId; DiscountItem has a conventional integer key without that suppression. Brand/type strings are non-Unicode, and product Price is configured with precision 19,4 as well as a money annotation [P1, P7-P10].

Caching Strategy

No explicit application cache provider, TTL, invalidation policy, distributed cache, or second-level cache appears in the traced data layer [P1, P12]. EF context tracking is not a documented shared result cache. Mock lists are the alternative implementation's sole data store, not cache-aside for SQL; no synchronization or persistence back to SQL is implemented [P2].

Data Ownership Boundaries

This is one catalog data owner, not database-per-microservice architecture. Desktop exchanges copied data contracts through WCF; service performs both reads and writes against the same context. No direct desktop cross-service database access, CQRS split, outbox, broker projection or cross-service aggregation is evidenced in this execution path [P11, P12].
